entries.d3a05c0aba2308d11ab479134425c1c3e0332331: <div sID="gen15207" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="2" osisID="Song.2" sID="Song.2"/> <div eID="gen15207" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15208" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen15209" type="x-p"/> In this chapter, I. Christ speaks both concerning himself and concerning his church, <reference osisRef="Song.2.1-Song.2.2">ver. 1, 2</reference>. II. The church speaks, 1. Remembering the pleasure and satisfaction she has in communion with Christ, <reference osisRef="Song.2.3-Song.2.4">ver. 3, 4</reference>. 2. Entertaining herself with the present tokens of his favour and taking care that nothing happen to intercept them, <reference osisRef="Song.2.5-Song.2.7">ver. 5-7</reference>. 3. Triumphing in his approaches towards her, <reference osisRef="Song.2.8-Song.2.9">ver. 8, 9</reference>. 4. Repeating the gracious calls he had given her to go along with him a walking, invited by the pleasures of the returning spring (<reference osisRef="Song.2.10-Song.2.13">ver. 10-13</reference>), out of her obscurity (<reference osisRef="Song.2.14">ver. 14</reference>), and the charge he had given to the servants to destroy that which would be hurtful to his vineyard, <reference osisRef="Song.2.15">ver. 15</reference>. 5. Rejoicing in her interest in him, <reference osisRef="Song.2.16">ver. 16</reference>. 6. Longing for his arrival, <reference osisRef="Song.2.17">ver. 17</reference>. Those whose hearts are filled with love to Christ, and hope of heaven, know best what these things mean.
entries.18c7fd844283e7ea74ae4f2a3c575faf1a232b37: <div eID="gen15209" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen15208" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">Christ the Rose of Sharon.</title> <div sID="gen15210" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> I <hi type="italic">am</hi> the rose of Sharon, <hi type="italic">and</hi> the lily of the valleys. <hi type="super">2</hi> As the lily among thorns, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> my love among the daughters. <div eID="gen15210" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15211" type="x-p"/> See here, I. What Christ is pleased to compare himself to; and he condescends very much in the comparison. He that is the Son of the Highest, the bright and morning star, calls and owns himself <hi type="italic">the rose of Sharon, and the lily of the valleys,</hi> to express his presence with his people in this world, the easiness of their access to him, and the beauty and sweetness which they find in him, and to teach them to adorn themselves with him, as shepherds and shepherdesses, when they appeared gay, were decked with roses and lilies, garlands and chaplets of flowers. <hi type="italic">The rose,</hi> for beauty and fragrance, is the chief of flowers, and our Saviour prefers the clothing of <hi type="italic">the lily</hi> before that of <hi type="italic">Solomon in all his glory.</hi> Christ is <hi type="italic">the rose of Sharon,</hi> where probably the best roses grew and in most plenty, <hi type="italic">the rose of the field</hi> (so some), denoting that the gospel salvation is a common salvation; it lies open to all; whoever will may come and gather the rose-buds of privileges and comforts that grow in the covenant of grace. He is not a rose locked up in a garden, but all may come and receive benefit by him and comfort in him. He is a <hi type="italic">lily</hi> for whiteness, a <hi type="italic">lily of the valleys</hi> for sweetness, for those which we call so yield a strong perfume. He is a <hi type="italic">lily of the valleys,</hi> or <hi type="italic">low places,</hi> in his humiliation, exposed to injury. Humble souls see most beauty in him. Whatever he is to others, to those that are in the <hi type="italic">valleys</hi> he is a <hi type="italic">lily.</hi> He is the <hi type="italic">rose, the lily;</hi> there is none besides. Whatever excellence is in Christ, it is in him singularly and in the highest degree. <div eID="gen15211" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15212" type="x-p"/> II. What he is pleased to compare his church to, <reference osisRef="Song.2.2">v. 2</reference>. 1. She is <hi type="italic">as a lily;</hi> he himself is <hi type="italic">the lily</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.2.1">v. 1</reference>), she is <hi type="italic">as the lily.</hi> The beauty of believers consists in their conformity and resemblance to Jesus Christ. They are his love, and so they are as lilies, for those are made like Christ in whose hearts his <hi type="italic">love is shed abroad.</hi> 2. <hi type="italic">As a lily among thorns, as a lily</hi> compared with <hi type="italic">thorns.</hi> The church of Christ as far excels all other societies as a bed of roses excels a bush of thorns. <hi type="italic">As a lily</hi> compassed with <hi type="italic">thorns.</hi> The wicked, the <hi type="italic">daughters</hi> of this world, such as have no love to Christ, are as <hi type="italic">thorns,</hi> worthless and useless, good for nothing but to stop a gap; nay, they are noxious and hurtful; they came in with sin and are a fruit of the curse; they choke good seed, and hinder good fruit, and their <hi type="italic">end is to be burned.</hi> God's people are <hi type="italic">as lilies among</hi> them, scratched and torn, shaded and obscured, by them; they are dear to Christ, and yet exposed to hardships and troubles in the world; they must expect it, for they are planted <hi type="italic">among thorns</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.2.6">Ezek. ii. 6</reference>), but they are nevertheless dear to him; he does not overlook nor undervalue any of his lilies for their being <hi type="italic">among thorns,</hi> When they are <hi type="italic">among thorns</hi> they must still be <hi type="italic">as lilies,</hi> must maintain their innocency and purity, and, though they are <hi type="italic">among thorns,</hi> must not be turned into <hi type="italic">thorns,</hi> must <hi type="italic">not render railing for railing,</hi> and, if they thus preserve their character, they shall be still owned as conformable to Christ. Grace in the soul is a <hi type="italic">lily among thorns;</hi> corruptions are <hi type="italic">thorns in the flesh</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2 Cor. xii. 7</reference>), are as Canaanites to God's Israel (<reference osisRef="Josh.23.13">Josh. xxiii. 13</reference>); but <hi type="italic">the lily</hi> that is now <hi type="italic">among thorns</hi> shall shortly be transplanted out of this wilderness into that paradise where there is no <hi type="italic">pricking brier</hi> nor <hi type="italic">grieving thorn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.28.24">Ezek. xxviii. 24</reference>.
entries.37aa719aa0a0fed4b20208a4bffc82b1a36c91f6: <div eID="gen15212" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15213" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">3</hi> As the apple tree among the trees of the wood, so <hi type="italic">is</hi> my beloved among the sons. I sat down under his shadow with great delight, and his fruit <hi type="italic">was</hi> sweet to my taste. 4 He brought me to the banqueting house, and his banner over me <hi type="italic">was</hi> love. <hi type="super">5</hi> Stay me with flagons, comfort me with apples: for I <hi type="italic">am</hi> sick of love. <hi type="super">6</hi> His left hand <hi type="italic">is</hi> under my head, and his right hand doth embrace me. <hi type="super">7</hi> I charge you, O ye daughters of Jerusalem, by the roes, and by the hinds of the field, that ye stir not up, nor awake <hi type="italic">my</hi> love, till he please. <div eID="gen15213" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15214" type="x-p"/> Here, I. The spouse commends her beloved and prefers him before all others: <hi type="italic">As the apple-tree among the trees of the wood,</hi> which perhaps does not grow so high, nor spread so wide, as some other trees, yet is useful and serviceable to man, yielding pleasant and profitable fruit, while the other trees are of little use, no, not the cedars themselves, till they are cut down, <hi type="italic">so is my beloved among the sons,</hi> so far does he excel them all,—all <hi type="italic">the sons</hi> of God, the angels (that honour was put upon him which was never designed for them, <reference osisRef="Heb.1.4">Heb. i. 4</reference>),—all <hi type="italic">the sons</hi> of men; he is <hi type="italic">fairer</hi> than them all, fairer than the choicest of them, <reference osisRef="Ps.45.2">Ps. xlv. 2</reference>. Name what creature you will, and you will find Christ has the pre-eminence above them all. The world is a barren tree to a soul; Christ is a fruitful one. <div eID="gen15214" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15215" type="x-p"/> II. She remembers the abundant comfort she has had in communion with him: She <hi type="italic">sat down</hi> by him <hi type="italic">with great delight,</hi> as shepherds sometimes repose themselves, sometimes converse with one another, under a tree. A double advantage she found in sitting down so near the Lord Jesus:—1. A refreshing shade: <hi type="italic">I sat down under his shadow,</hi> to be sheltered by him from the scorching heat of the sun, to be cooled, and so to take some rest. Christ is to believers <hi type="italic">as the shadow</hi> of a great tree, nay, <hi type="italic">of a great rock in a weary land,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Isa. xxxii. 2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">xxv. 4</reference>. When a poor soul is parched with convictions of sin and the terrors of the law, as David (<reference osisRef="Ps.32.4">Ps. xxxii. 4</reference>), when fatigued with the troubles of this world, as Elijah when he <hi type="italic">sat down under a juniper tree</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.4">1 Kings xix. 4</reference>), they find that in Christ, in his name, his graces, his comforts, and his undertaking for poor sinners, which revives them and keeps them from fainting; those that <hi type="italic">are weary and heavily laden</hi> may find <hi type="italic">rest</hi> in Christ. It is not enough to pass by this <hi type="italic">shadow,</hi> but we must <hi type="italic">sit down under</hi> it (<hi type="italic">here will I dwell, for I have desired it</hi>); and we shall find it not like Jonah's gourd, that soon withered, and left him in a heat, both inward and outward, but like the tree of life, the leaves whereof were not only for shelter, but for the healing of the nations. We must <hi type="italic">sit down under this shadow with delight,</hi> must put an entire confidence in the protection of it (as <reference osisRef="Judg.9.15">Judges ix. 15</reference>), and take an entire complacency in the refreshment of it. But that is not all: 2. Here is pleasing nourishing food. This tree drops its fruits to those that <hi type="italic">sit down under its shadow,</hi> and they are welcome to them, and will find them <hi type="italic">sweet unto their taste,</hi> whatever they are to others. Believers have tasted that the Lord Jesus is <hi type="italic">gracious</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.3">1 Pet. ii. 3</reference>); his <hi type="italic">fruits</hi> are all the precious privileges of the new covenant, purchased by his blood and communicated by his Spirit. Promises are sweet to a believer, yea, and precepts too. <hi type="italic">I delight in the law of God after the inward man.</hi> Pardons are sweet, and peace of conscience is sweet, assurances of God's love, joys of the Holy Ghost, the hopes of eternal life, and the present earnests and foretastes of it are sweet, all sweet to those that have their spiritual senses exercised. If our mouths be put out of taste for the pleasure of sin, divine consolations will be <hi type="italic">sweet to our taste, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.</hi> <div eID="gen15215" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15216" type="x-p"/> III. She owns herself obliged to Jesus Christ for all the benefit and comfort she had in communion with him (<reference osisRef="Song.2.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">I sat down under</hi> the apple-tree, glad to be there, but he admitted me, nay, he pressed me, to a more intimate communion with him: <hi type="italic">Come in, thou blessed of the Lord, why standest thou without?</hi> <hi type="italic">He brought me to the house</hi> of wine, the place where he entertains his special friends, from lower to higher measures and degrees of comfort, from the fruit of the <hi type="italic">apple tree</hi> to the more generous fruit of the vine." <hi type="italic">To him that</hi> values the divine joys he <hi type="italic">has more shall be given.</hi> One of the rabbin by <hi type="italic">the banqueting-house</hi> understands the <hi type="italic">tabernacle of the congregation, where the interpretation of the law was given;</hi> surely we may apply it to Christian assemblies, where the gospel is preached and gospel-ordinances are administered, particularly the Lord's supper, that <hi type="italic">banquet of wine,</hi> especially to the inside of those ordinances, communion with God in them. Observe, 1. How she was introduced: "<hi type="italic">He brought me,</hi> wrought in me an inclination to draw nigh to God, helped me over my discouragements, took me by the hand, guided and led me, and gave me an <hi type="italic">access</hi> with boldness to God as a <hi type="italic">Father,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Eph.2.18">Eph. ii. 18</reference>. We should never have come <hi type="italic">into the banqueting-house,</hi> never have been acquainted with spiritual pleasures, if Christ had not brought us, by opening for us a new and living way and opening in us a new and living fountain. 2. How she was entertained: <hi type="italic">His banner over me was love; he brought me</hi> in with a banner displayed over my head, not as one he triumphed over, but as one he triumphed in, and whom he always caused to triumph with him and in him, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.14">2 Cor. ii. 14</reference>. The gospel is compared to a <hi type="italic">banner</hi> or <hi type="italic">ensign</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.11.12">Isa. xi. 12</reference>), and that which is represented in the banner, written in it in letters of gold, letters of blood, is <hi type="italic">love, love;</hi> and this is the entertainment in <hi type="italic">the banqueting-house.</hi> Christ is the <hi type="italic">captain of our salvation,</hi> and he enlists all his soldiers under the <hi type="italic">banner of love;</hi> in that they centre; to that they must continually have an eye, and be animated by it. <hi type="italic">The love of Christ</hi> must <hi type="italic">constrain</hi> them to fight manfully. When a city was taken the conqueror set up his standard in it. "He has conquered me with his love, overcome me with kindness, and that is the <hi type="italic">banner over me.</hi>" This she speaks of as what she had formerly had experience of, and she remembers it with delight. Eaten bread must not be forgotten, but remembered with thankfulness to that God who has fed us with manna in this wilderness. <div eID="gen15216" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15217" type="x-p"/> IV. She professes her strong affection and most passionate love to Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Song.2.5">v. 5</reference>): <hi type="italic">I am sick of love,</hi> overcome, overpowered, by it. David explains this when he says (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.20">Ps. cxix. 20</reference>), <hi type="italic">My soul breaks for the longing that it has unto thy judgments,</hi> and (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.81">v. 81</reference>), <hi type="italic">My soul faints for thy salvation,</hi> languishing with care to make it sure and fear of coming short of it. The spouse was now absent perhaps from her beloved, waiting for his return, and cannot bear the grief of distance and delay. Oh how much better it is with the soul when it is <hi type="italic">sick of love</hi> to Christ than when it is surfeited with the love of this world! She cries out for cordials: "Oh <hi type="italic">stay me with flagons,</hi> or <hi type="italic">ointments,</hi> or <hi type="italic">flowers,</hi> any thing that is reviving; <hi type="italic">comfort me with apples,</hi> with the fruits of that <hi type="italic">apple-tree,</hi> Christ (<reference osisRef="Song.2.3">v. 3</reference>), with the merit and meditation of Christ and the sense of his love to my soul." Note, Those that are <hi type="italic">sick of love</hi> to Christ shall not want spiritual supports, while they are yet waiting for spiritual comforts. <div eID="gen15217" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15218" type="x-p"/> V. She experiences the power and tenderness of divine grace, relieving her in her present faintings, <reference osisRef="Song.2.6">v. 6</reference>. Though he seemed to have withdrawn, yet he was even then a very present help, 1. To sustain the love-sick soul, and to keep it from fainting away: "<hi type="italic">His left hand is under my head,</hi> to bear it up, nay, as a pillow to lay it easy." David experienced God's hand upholding him then when <hi type="italic">his soul was following hard after God</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.63.8">Ps. lxiii. 8</reference>), and Job in a state of desertion yet found that God <hi type="italic">put strength</hi> into him, <reference osisRef="Job.23.6">Job xxiii. 6</reference>. <hi type="italic">All his saints are in his hand,</hi> which tenderly holds their aching heads. 2. To encourage the love-sick soul to continue waiting till he returns: "For, in the mean time, <hi type="italic">his right hand embraces me,</hi> and thereby gives me an unquestionable assurance of his love." Believers owe all their strength and comfort to the supporting left hand and embracing right hand of the Lord Jesus. <div eID="gen15218" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15219" type="x-p"/> VI. Finding her beloved thus nigh unto her she is in great care that her communion with him be not interrupted (<reference osisRef="Song.2.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">I charge you, O you daughters of Jerusalem.</hi> Jerusalem, the mother of us all, charges all her daughters, the church charges all her members, the believing soul charges all its powers and faculties, the spouse charges herself and all about her, not to <hi type="italic">stir up, or awake, her love until he please,</hi> now that he is asleep in her arms, as she was borne up in his, <reference osisRef="Song.2.6">v. 6</reference>. She gives them this charge <hi type="italic">by the roes and the hinds of the field,</hi> that is, by every thing that is amiable in their eyes, and dear to them, <hi type="italic">as the loving hind and the pleasant roe.</hi> "My love is to me dearer than those can be to you, and will be disturbed, like them, with a very little noise." Note, 1. Those that experience the sweetness of communion with Christ, and the sensible manifestations of his love, cannot but desire the continuance of these blessed views, these blessed visits. Peter would make tabernacles upon the holy mount, <reference osisRef="Matt.17.4">Matt. xvii. 4</reference>. 2. Yet Christ will, when he pleases, withdraw those extraordinary communications of himself, for he is a free-agent, and the Spirit, as <hi type="italic">the wind, blows where</hi> and when <hi type="italic">it listeth,</hi> and in his pleasure it becomes us to acquiesce. But, 3. Our care must be that we do nothing to provoke him to withdraw and to hide his face, that we carefully watch over our own hearts and suppress every thought that may grieve his good Spirit. Let those that have comfort be afraid of sinning it away.
entries.fb5226b1ff2655e7e86b4b2065adb550072d4198: <div eID="gen15219" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">Mutual Love of Christ and the Church.</title> <div sID="gen15220" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">8</hi> The voice of my beloved! behold, he cometh leaping upon the mountains, skipping upon the hills. <hi type="super">9</hi> My beloved is like a roe or a young hart: behold, he standeth behind our wall, he looketh forth at the windows, showing himself through the lattice. <hi type="super">10</hi> My beloved spake, and said unto me, Rise up, my love, my fair one, and come away. <hi type="super">11</hi> For, lo, the winter is past, the rain is over <hi type="italic">and</hi> gone; <hi type="super">12</hi> The flowers appear on the earth; the time of the singing <hi type="italic">of birds</hi> is come, and the voice of the turtle is heard in our land; <hi type="super">13</hi> The fig tree putteth forth her green figs, and the vines <hi type="italic">with</hi> the tender grape give a <hi type="italic">good</hi> smell. Arise, my love, my fair one, and come away. <div eID="gen15220" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15221" type="x-p"/> The church is here pleasing herself exceedingly with the thoughts of her further communion with Christ after she has recovered from her fainting fit. <div eID="gen15221" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15222" type="x-p"/> I. She rejoices in his approach, <reference osisRef="Song.2.8">v. 8</reference>. 1. She hears him speak: "It is <hi type="italic">the voice of my beloved,</hi> calling me to tell me he is coming." Like one of his own sheep, she <hi type="italic">knows his voice</hi> before she sees him, and can easily distinguish it from the <hi type="italic">voice of a stranger</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.10.4-John.10.5">John x. 4, 5</reference>), and, like a faithful friend of the bridegroom, she <hi type="italic">rejoices greatly because of the bridegroom's voice,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.3.29">John iii. 29</reference>. With what an air of triumph and exultation does she cry out, "<hi type="italic">It is the voice of my beloved,</hi> it can be the voice of no other, for none besides can speak to the heart and make that burn." 2. She sees him come, sees the goings of <hi type="italic">our God, our King,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.48.24">Ps. xlviii. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">Behold, he comes.</hi> This may very well be applied to the prospect with the Old-Testament saints had of Christ's coming in the flesh. <hi type="italic">Abraham saw his day</hi> at a distance, <hi type="italic">and was glad.</hi> The nearer the time came the clearer discoveries were made of it; and those that waited for the consolation of Israel with an eye of faith saw him come, and triumphed in the sight: <hi type="italic">Behold, he comes;</hi> for they had heard him say (<reference osisRef="Ps.40.7">Ps. xl. 7</reference>), <hi type="italic">Lo, I come,</hi> to which their faith here affixes its seal: <hi type="italic">Behold, he comes</hi> as he has promised. (1.) He comes cheerfully and with great alacrity; he comes leaping and skipping <hi type="italic">like a roe</hi> and like <hi type="italic">a young hart</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.2.9">v. 9</reference>), as one pleased with his own undertaking, and that had his heart upon it and his delights with the sons of men. When he came to be baptized with the baptism of blood, how was he <hi type="italic">straitened till it was accomplished!</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.50">Luke xii. 50</reference>. (2.) He comes slighting and surmounting all the difficulties that lay in his way; he comes <hi type="italic">leaping over the mountains, skipping over the hills</hi> (so some read it), making nothing of the discouragements he was to break through; the curse of the law, the death of the cross, must be undergone, all the powers of darkness must be grappled with, but, before the resolutions of his love, these great mountains become plains. Whatever opposition is given at any time to the deliverance of God's church, Christ will break through it, will get over it. (3.) He comes speedily, <hi type="italic">like a roe</hi> or <hi type="italic">a young hart;</hi> they thought the time long (every day a year), but really he hastened; as now, so then, <hi type="italic">surely he comes quickly; he that shall come will come, and will not tarry.</hi> When he comes for the deliverance of his people he <hi type="italic">flies upon a cloud,</hi> and never stays beyond his time, which is the best time. We may apply it to particular believers, who find that even when Christ has withdrawn sensible comforts, and seems to forsake, yet it is but for a small moment, and he will soon return with everlasting loving-kindness. <div eID="gen15222" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15223" type="x-p"/> II. She pleases herself with the glimpses she has of him, and the glances she has of his favour: "He <hi type="italic">stands behind our wall;</hi> I know he is there, for sometimes <hi type="italic">he looks forth at the window,</hi> or <hi type="italic">looks in</hi> at it, and displays <hi type="italic">himself through the lattice.</hi>" Such was the state of the Old-Testament church while it was in expectation of the coming of the Messiah. The ceremonial law is called <hi type="italic">a wall of partition</hi> (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Eph. ii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">a veil</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.13">2 Cor. iii. 13</reference>); but Christ stood behind that wall. They had him near them; they had him with them, though they could not see him clearly. He that was the substance was not far off from the shadows, <reference osisRef="Col.2.17">Col. ii. 17</reference>. The saw him looking through the windows of the ceremonial institutions and smiling through those lattices; in their sacrifices and purifications Christ discovered himself to them, and gave them intimations and earnests of his grace, both to engage and to encourage their longings for his coming. Such is our present state in comparison with what it will be at Christ's second coming. We now <hi type="italic">see him through a glass darkly</hi> (the body is a wall between us and him, through the windows of which we now and then get a sight of him), but not <hi type="italic">face to face,</hi> as we hope to see him shortly. In the sacraments Christ is near us, but it is <hi type="italic">behind the wall</hi> of external signs, through <hi type="italic">those lattices</hi> he manifests himself to us; but we shall shortly <hi type="italic">see him as he is.</hi> Some understand this of the state of a believer when he is under a cloud; Christ is out of sight and yet not far off. See <reference osisRef="Job.34.14">Job xxxiv. 14</reference>, and compare <reference osisRef="Job.23.8-Job.23.10">Job xxiii. 8-10</reference>. She calls the wall that interposed between her and her beloved <hi type="italic">our wall,</hi> because it is sin, and nothing else, that separates between us and God, and that is a wall of our own erecting (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.1">Isa. lix. 1</reference>); behind that he stands, as <hi type="italic">waiting to be gracious,</hi> and ready to be reconciled, upon our repentance. Then <hi type="italic">he looks in at the window,</hi> observes the frame of our hearts and the working of our souls; he looks forth at the window, and shows himself in giving them some comfort, that they may continue hoping for his return. <div eID="gen15223" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15224" type="x-p"/> III. She repeats the gracious invitation he had given her to come a walking with him, <reference osisRef="Song.2.10-Song.2.13">v. 10-13</reference>. She remembers what her beloved said to her, for it had made a very pleasing and powerful impression upon her, and the <hi type="italic">word that quickens us</hi> we shall <hi type="italic">never forget.</hi> She relates it for the encouragement of others, telling them what he had said to her soul and <hi type="italic">done for her soul,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.66.16">Ps. lxvi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen15224" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15225" type="x-p"/> 1. He called her his love and his fair one. Whatever she is to others, to him she is acceptable, and in his eyes she is amiable. Those that take Christ for their beloved, he will own as his; never was any love lost that was bestowed upon Christ. Christ, by expressing his love to believers, invites and encourages them to follow him. <div eID="gen15225" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15226" type="x-p"/> 2. He called her to <hi type="italic">rise and come away,</hi> <reference osisRef="Song.2.10">v. 10</reference>, and again <reference osisRef="Song.2.13">v. 13</reference>. The repetition denotes backwardness in her (we have need to be often called to come away with Jesus Christ; <hi type="italic">precept must be upon precept and line upon line</hi>), but it denotes earnestness in him; so much is his heart set upon the welfare of precious souls that he importunes them most pressingly to that which is for their own good. <div eID="gen15226" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15227" type="x-p"/> 3. He gave for a reason the return of the spring, and the pleasantness of the weather. <div eID="gen15227" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15228" type="x-p"/> (1.) The season is elegantly described in a great variety of expressions. [1.] <hi type="italic">The winter is past,</hi> the dark, cold, and barren winter. Long winters and hard ones pass away at last; they do no endure always. And the spring would not be so pleasant as it is if it did not succeed the winter, which is a foil to its beauty, <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.14">Eccl. vii. 14</reference>. Neither the face of the heavens nor that of the earth is always the same, but subject to continual vicissitudes, diurnal and annual. <hi type="italic">The winter is past,</hi> but has not passed away for ever; it will come again, and we must provide for it in summer, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.6">Prov. vi. 6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Prov.6.8">8</reference>. We must weep in winter, and rejoice in summer, as though we wept and rejoiced not, for both are passing. [2.] <hi type="italic">The rain is over and gone,</hi> the winter-rain, the cold stormy rain; it is over now, and <hi type="italic">the dew is as the dew of herbs.</hi> Even the rain that drowned the world was over and gone at last (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.1-Gen.8.3">Gen. viii. 1-3</reference>), and God promised to drown the world no more, which was a type and figure of the covenant of grace, <reference osisRef="Isa.54.9">Isa. liv. 9</reference>. [3.] <hi type="italic">The flowers appear on the earth.</hi> All winter they are dead and buried in their roots, and there is no sign of them; but in the spring they revive, and show themselves in a wonderful variety and verdure, and, like the dew that produces them, <hi type="italic">tarry not for man,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mic.5.7">Mic. v. 7</reference>. They appear, but they will soon disappear again, and man in herein like <hi type="italic">the flower of the field,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.14.2">Job xiv. 2</reference>. [4.] <hi type="italic">The time of singing of birds has come.</hi> The little birds, which all the winter lie hid in their retirements and scarcely live, when the spring returns forget all the calamities of the winter, and to the best of their capacity chant forth the praises of their Creator. Doubtless he who understands the birds that cry for want (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.9">Ps. cxlvii. 9</reference>) takes notice of those that <hi type="italic">sing for joy</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.104.12">Ps. civ. 12</reference>. The singing of the birds may shame our silence in God's praises, who are better fed (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.26">Matt. vi. 26</reference>), and better taught (<reference osisRef="Job.35.11">Job xxxv. 11</reference>), and are of <hi type="italic">more value than many sparrows.</hi> They live without inordinate care (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.26">Matt. vi. 26</reference>) and therefore they sing, while we murmur. [5.] <hi type="italic">The voice of the turtle is heard in our land,</hi> which is one of the season-birds mentioned <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jer. viii. 7</reference>, that observe the time of their coming and the time of their singing, and so shame us who <hi type="italic">know not the judgment of the Lord,</hi> understand not the times, nor do that which is <hi type="italic">beautiful in its season,</hi> do not sing in singing time. [6.] <hi type="italic">The fig-tree puts forth her green figs,</hi> by which <hi type="italic">we know that summer is nigh</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.32">Matt. xxiv. 32</reference>), when the green figs will be ripe figs and fit for use; and the <hi type="italic">vines with the tender grape give a good smell.</hi> The earth produces not only <hi type="italic">flowers</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.2.12">v. 12</reference>), but <hi type="italic">fruits;</hi> and the smell of the fruits, which are profitable, is to be preferred far before that of the flowers, which are only for show and pleasure. Serpents, they say, are driven away by the smell of the vines; and who is the old serpent, and who the true vine, we know very well. <div eID="gen15228" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15229" type="x-p"/> (2.) Now this description of the returning spring, as a reason for coming away with Christ, is applicable [1.] To the introducing of the gospel in the room of the Old-Testament dispensation, during which it had been winter time with the church. Christ's gospel warms that which was cold, makes that fruitful which before was dead and barren; when it comes to any place it puts a beauty and glory upon that place (<reference osisRef="2Cor.3.7-2Cor.3.8">2 Cor. iii. 7, 8</reference>) and furnishes occasion for joy. Spring-time is pleasant time, and so is gospel-time. <hi type="italic">Aspice venturo lætentur ut omnia seclo</hi>—<hi type="italic">Behold what joy the dawning age inspires!</hi> said Virgil, from the Sibyls, perhaps with more reference to the setting up of the Messiah's kingdom at that time than he himself thought of. See <reference osisRef="Ps.96.11">Ps. xcvi. 11</reference>. <hi type="italic">Arise then,</hi> and improve this spring-time. <hi type="italic">Come away</hi> from the world and the flesh, come into <hi type="italic">fellowship with Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.9">1 Cor. i. 9</reference>. [2.] To the delivering of the church from the power of persecuting enemies, and the restoring of liberty and peace to it, after a severe winter of suffering and restraint. When the storms of trouble are over and gone, when the <hi type="italic">voice of the turtle,</hi> the joyful sound of the gospel of Christ, is again heard, and ordinances are enjoyed with freedom, then <hi type="italic">arise and come away</hi> to improve the happy juncture. Walk in the light of the Lord; sing in the ways of the Lord. When the churches had rest, then were they edified, <reference osisRef="Acts.9.31">Acts ix. 31</reference>. [3.] To the conversion of sinners from a state of nature to a state of grace. That blessed change is like the return of the spring, a universal change and a very comfortable one; it is a new creation; it is being born again. The soul that was hard, and cold, and frozen, and unprofitable, like the earth in winter, becomes fruitful, like the earth in spring, and by degrees, like it, brings its fruits to perfection. This blessed change is owing purely to the approaches and influences of the sun of righteousness, who calls to us from heaven to <hi type="italic">arise and come away;</hi> come, gather in summer. [4.] To the consolations of the saints after a state of inward dejection and despondency. A child of God, under doubts and fears, is like the earth in winter, its nights long, its days dark, good affections chilled, nothing done, nothing got, the hand sealed up. But comfort will return; the birds shall sing again, and the flowers appear. Arise therefore, poor drooping soul, and <hi type="italic">come away</hi> with thy beloved. <hi type="italic">Arise, and shake thyself from the dust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.52.2">Isa. lii. 2</reference>. <hi type="italic">Arise, shine, for thy light has come</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.1">Isa. lx. 1</reference>); <hi type="italic">walk in that light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.2.5">Isa. ii. 5</reference>. [5.] To the resurrection of the body at the last day, and the glory to be revealed. The bones that lay in the grave, as the roots of the plants in the ground during the winter, shall then <hi type="italic">flourish as a herb,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.66.14">Isa. lxvi. 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.26.19">xxvi. 19</reference>. That will be an eternal farewell to winter and a joyful entrance upon an everlasting spring.
entries.b92f0fd5f7f1620f43f73e99455ac5a788d33e61: <div eID="gen15229" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Love of the Church to Christ.</title> <div sID="gen15230" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> O my dove, <hi type="italic">that art</hi> in the clefts of the rock, in the secret <hi type="italic">places</hi> of the stairs, let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice; for sweet <hi type="italic">is</hi> thy voice, and thy countenance <hi type="italic">is</hi> comely. <hi type="super">15</hi> Take us the foxes, the little foxes, that spoil the vines: for our vines <hi type="italic">have</hi> tender grapes. <hi type="super">16</hi> My beloved <hi type="italic">is</hi> mine, and I <hi type="italic">am</hi> his: he feedeth among the lilies. <hi type="super">17</hi> Until the day break, and the shadows flee away, turn, my beloved, and be thou like a roe or a young hart upon the mountains of Bether. <div eID="gen15230" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15231" type="x-p"/> Here is, I. The encouraging invitation which Christ gives to the church, and every believing soul, to come into communion with him, <reference osisRef="Song.2.14">v. 14</reference>. <div eID="gen15231" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15232" type="x-p"/> 1. His love is now his <hi type="italic">dove;</hi> David had called the church God's <hi type="italic">turtle-dove</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.19">Ps. lxxxiv. 19</reference>), and so she is here called; a dove for beauty, her <hi type="italic">wings covered with silver</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.13">Ps. xviii. 13</reference>), for innocence and inoffensiveness; a gracious spirit is a dove-like spirit, harmless, loving quietness and cleanliness, and faithful to Christ, as the turtle to her mate. The Spirit descended <hi type="italic">like a dove</hi> on Christ, and so he does on all Christians, making them of a <hi type="italic">meek and quiet spirit.</hi> She is Christ's <hi type="italic">dove,</hi> for he owns her and delights in her; she can find no rest but in him and his ark, and therefore to him, as her Noah, she returns. <div eID="gen15232" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15233" type="x-p"/> 2. This dove is <hi type="italic">in the clefts of the rock and in the secret places of the stairs.</hi> This speaks either, (1.) Her praise. Christ is the rock, to whom she flies for shelter and in whom alone she can think herself safe and find herself easy, as a dove in the hole of a rock, when struck at by the birds of prey, <reference osisRef="Jer.48.28">Jer. xlviii. 28</reference>. Moses was hid in a cleft of the rock, that he might behold something of God's glory, which otherwise he could not have borne the brightness of. She retires <hi type="italic">into the secret places of the stairs,</hi> where she may be alone, undisturbed, and may the better commune with her own heart. Good Christians will find time to be private. Christ often withdrew to a mountain <hi type="italic">himself alone, to pray.</hi> Or, (2.) her blame. She crept into the <hi type="italic">clefts of the rock,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">secret places,</hi> for fear and shame, any where to hide her head, being heartless and discouraged, and shunning even the sight of her beloved. Being conscious to herself of her own unfitness and unworthiness to come into his presence, and speak to him, she drew back, and was <hi type="italic">like a silly dove without heart,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hos.7.11">Hos. vii. 11</reference>. <div eID="gen15233" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15234" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ graciously calls her out of her retirements: Come, <hi type="italic">let me see thy countenance, let me hear thy voice.</hi> She was <hi type="italic">mourning like a dove</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Isa. xxxviii. 14</reference>), bemoaning herself like the <hi type="italic">doves of the valleys,</hi> where they are near the clefts of the impending rocks, <hi type="italic">mourning for her iniquities</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16">Ezek. vii. 16</reference>) and refusing to be comforted. But Christ calls her to <hi type="italic">lift up her face without spot,</hi> being purged from an evil conscience (<reference osisRef="Job.11.15">Job xi. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.26">xxii. 26</reference>), to <hi type="italic">come boldly to the throne of grace,</hi> having a great <hi type="italic">high priest</hi> there (<reference osisRef="Heb.4.16">Heb. iv. 16</reference>), to tell what her petition is and what her request: Let me <hi type="italic">hear thy voice,</hi> hear what thou hast to say; <hi type="italic">what would you that I should do unto you?</hi> Speak freely, speak up, and fear not a slight or repulse. <div eID="gen15234" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15235" type="x-p"/> 4. For her encouragement, he tells her the good thoughts he had of her, whatever she thought of herself: <hi type="italic">Sweet is thy voice;</hi> thy praying voice, though thou canst but <hi type="italic">chatter like a crane or a swallow</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.38.14">Isa. xxxviii. 14</reference>); it is music in God's ears. He has assured us that <hi type="italic">the prayer of the upright is his delight;</hi> he smelled a sweet savour from Noah's sacrifice, and the <hi type="italic">spiritual sacrifices</hi> are no less <hi type="italic">acceptable,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.5">1 Pet. ii. 5</reference>. This does not so much commend our services as God's gracious condescension in making the best of them, and the efficacy of the <hi type="italic">much incense</hi> which is <hi type="italic">offered with the prayers of saints,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.8.3">Rev. viii. 3</reference>. "That countenance of thine, which thou art ashamed of, is comely, though now mournful, much more will it be so when it becomes cheerful." <hi type="italic">Then</hi> the voice of prayer is sweet and acceptable to God when the countenance, the conversation in which we show ourselves before men, is holy, and so comely, and agreeable to our profession. Those that are sanctified have the best comeliness. <div eID="gen15235" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15236" type="x-p"/> II. The charge which Christ gives to his servants to oppose and suppress that which is a terror to his church and drives her, like a poor frightened dove, into the clefts of the rock, and which is an obstruction and prejudice to the interests of his kingdom in this world and in the heart (<reference osisRef="Song.2.15">v. 15</reference>): <hi type="italic">Take us the foxes</hi> (take them for us, for it is good service both to Christ and the church), <hi type="italic">the little foxes,</hi> that creep in insensibly; for, though they are little, they do great mischief, they <hi type="italic">spoil the vines,</hi> which they must by no means be suffered to do at any time, especially now when our vines have <hi type="italic">tender grapes</hi> that must be preserved, or the vintage will fail. Believers are as vines, weak but useful plants; their fruits are as <hi type="italic">tender crops</hi> at first, which must have time to come to maturity. This charge to <hi type="italic">take the foxes</hi> is, 1. A charge to particular believers to mortify their own corruptions, their sinful appetites and passions, which are as <hi type="italic">foxes, little foxes,</hi> that destroy their graces and comforts, quash good motions, crush good beginnings, and prevent their coming to perfection. Seize the <hi type="italic">little foxes,</hi> the first risings of sin, the little ones of Babylon (<reference osisRef="Ps.137.9">Ps. cxxxvii. 9</reference>), those sins that seem little, for they often prove very dangerous. Whatever we find a hindrance to us in that which is good we must put away. 2. A charge to all in their places to oppose and prevent the spreading of all such opinions and practices as tend to corrupt men's judgments, debauch their consciences, perplex their minds, and discourage their inclinations to virtue and piety. Persecutors are foxes (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.32">Luke xiii. 32</reference>); false prophets are foxes, <reference osisRef="Ezek.13.4">Eze. xiii. 4</reference>. Those that sow the tares of heresy or schism, and, like Diotrephes, trouble the peace of the church and obstruct the progress of the gospel, they are the <hi type="italic">foxes, the little foxes,</hi> which must not be knocked on the head (<hi type="italic">Christ came not to destroy men's lives</hi>), but taken, that they may be tamed, or else restrained from doing mischief. <div eID="gen15236" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15237" type="x-p"/> III. The believing profession which the church makes of her relation to Christ, and the satisfaction she takes in her interest in him and communion with him, <reference osisRef="Song.2.16">v. 16</reference>. He had called her to <hi type="italic">rise</hi> and <hi type="italic">come away</hi> with him, to let him see her face and hear her voice; now this is her answer to that call, in which, though at present in the dark and at a distance, <div eID="gen15237" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15238" type="x-p"/> 1. She comforts herself with the thoughts of the mutual interest and relation that were between her and her beloved: <hi type="italic">My beloved to me</hi> and <hi type="italic">I to him,</hi> so the original reads it very emphatically; the conciseness of the language speaks the largeness of her affection: "What he is to me and I to him may better be conceived than expressed." Note, (1.) It is the unspeakable privilege of true believers that Christ is theirs: <hi type="italic">My beloved is mine;</hi> this denotes not only propriety ("I have a title to him") but possession and tenure—"I receive from his fulness." Believers are partakers of Christ; they have not only an interest in him, but the enjoyment of him, are taken not only in the covenant, but into communion with him. All the benefits of his glorious undertaking, as Mediator, are made over to them. He is that to them which the world neither is nor can be, all that which they need and desire, and which will make a complete happiness for them. All he is is theirs, and all he has, all he has done, and all he is doing; all he has promised in the gospel, all he has prepared in heaven, all is yours. (2.) It is the undoubted character of all true believers that they are Christ's, and then, and then only, he is theirs. They have given their own selves to him (<reference osisRef="2Cor.8.5">2 Cor. viii. 5</reference>); they receive his doctrine and obey his laws; they bear his image and espouse his interest; they belong to Christ. If we be his, his wholly, his only, his for ever, we may take the comfort of his being ours. <div eID="gen15238" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15239" type="x-p"/> 2. She comforts herself with the thoughts of the communications of his grace to his people: <hi type="italic">He feeds among the lilies.</hi> When she wants the tokens of his favour to her in particular, she rejoices in the assurance of his presence with all believers in general, who are lilies in his eyes. He <hi type="italic">feeds</hi> among them, that is, he takes as much pleasure in them and their assemblies as a man does in his table or in his garden, for he <hi type="italic">walks in the midst of the golden candlesticks;</hi> he delights to converse with them, and to do them good. <div eID="gen15239" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen15240" type="x-p"/> IV. The church's hope and expectation of Christ's coming, and her prayer grounded thereupon. 1. She doubts not but that the <hi type="italic">day will break</hi> and the <hi type="italic">shadows</hi> will <hi type="italic">flee away.</hi> The gospel-day will dawn, and the shadows of the ceremonial law will flee away. This was the comfort of the Old-Testament church, that, after the long night of that dark dispensation, the <hi type="italic">day-spring from on high would</hi> at length <hi type="italic">visit them,</hi> to <hi type="italic">give light to those that sit in darkness.</hi> When the sun rises the shades of the night vanish, so do the shadows of the day when the substance comes. The day of comfort will come after a night of desertion. Or it may refer to the second coming of Christ, and the eternal happiness of the saints; the shadows of our present state will flee away, our darkness and doubts, our griefs and all our grievances, and a glorious day shall dawn, a morning when the <hi type="italic">upright shall have dominion,</hi> a day that shall have no night after it. 2. She begs the presence of her beloved, in the mean time, to support and comfort her: "<hi type="italic">Turn, my beloved,</hi> turn to me, come and visit me, come and relieve me, <hi type="italic">be with me always to the end of the age.</hi> In the day of my extremity, make haste to help me, <hi type="italic">make no long tarrying.</hi> Come over even <hi type="italic">the mountains of division,</hi> interposing time and days, with some gracious anticipations of that light and love." 3. She begs that he would not only turn to her for the present, but hasten his coming to fetch her to himself. <hi type="italic">"Even so, come, Lord Jesus, come quickly.</hi> Though there be mountains in the way, thou canst, <hi type="italic">like a roe, or a young hart,</hi> step over them with ease. <hi type="italic">O show thyself to me, or take me up to thee.</hi>"  <chapter eID="Song.2"/> <div eID="gen15240" type="x-p"/>

entries.890e481c442dd0157beaa2c032bca7b9fb609674: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8209"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 2</title> <div sID="gen12888" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Song.2.1-Song.2.17">So 2:1-17</reference>.<div eID="gen12888" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12889" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8209"/><hi type="bold">1. rose--</hi>if applied to Jesus Christ, it, with the white lily (lowly, <reference osisRef="2Cor.8.9">2Co 8:9</reference>), answers to "white and ruddy" (<reference osisRef="Song.5.10">So 5:10</reference>). But it is rather the meadow-saffron: the Hebrew means radically a plant with a pungent bulb, inapplicable to the rose. So Syriac. It is of a white and violet color [Maurer, Gesenius, and Weiss]. The bride thus speaks of herself as lowly though lovely, in contrast with the lordly "apple" or citron tree, the bridegroom (<reference osisRef="Song.2.3">So 2:3</reference>); so the "lily" is applied to her (<reference osisRef="Song.2.2">So 2:2</reference>),<div eID="gen12889" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12890" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Sharon--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Isa.35.1">Is 35:1</reference>, 2). In North Palestine, between Mount Tabor and Lake Tiberias (<reference osisRef="1Chr.5.16">1Ch 5:16</reference>). Septuagint and Vulgate translate it, "a plain"; though they err in this, the Hebrew Bible not elsewhere favoring it, yet the parallelism to valleys shows that, in the proper name Sharon, there is here a tacit reference to its meaning of lowliness. Beauty, delicacy, and lowliness, are to be in her, as they were in Him (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.29">Mt 11:29</reference>). <div eID="gen12890" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf344938d02bc0634773f9a64adb08c5db73a434: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8210"/><div sID="gen12891" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8210"/>2. Jesus Christ to the Bride (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Mt 10:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.15.19">Joh 15:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.5.19">1Jo 5:19</reference>). Thorns, equivalent to the wicked (<reference osisRef="2Sam.23.6">2Sa 23:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.57.4">Psa 57:4</reference>).<div eID="gen12891" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12892" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">daughters--</hi>of men, not of God; not "the virgins." "If thou art the lily of Jesus Christ, take heed lest by impatience, rash judgments, and pride, thou thyself become a thorn" [Luther]. <div eID="gen12892" type="x-p"/>
entries.04b8683f37f7602c633a2b0e73a3603409fd5a09: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8211"/><div sID="gen12893" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8211"/><hi type="bold">3. Her reply. apple--</hi>generic including the golden citron, pomegranate, and orange apple (<reference osisRef="Prov.25.11">Pr 25:11</reference>). He combines the shadow and fragrance of the citron with the sweetness of the orange and pomegranate fruit. The foliage is perpetual; throughout the year a succession of blossoms, fruit, and perfume (<reference osisRef="Jas.1.17">Jas 1:17</reference>).<div eID="gen12893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">among the sons--</hi>parallel to "among the daughters" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.2">So 2:2</reference>). He alone is ever fruitful among the fruitless wild trees (<reference osisRef="Ps.89.6">Psa 89:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.9">He 1:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12894" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12895" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">I sat ... with ... delight--</hi>literally, "I eagerly desired and sat" (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.19">Psa 94:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.6.31">Mr 6:31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.2.6">Ep 2:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.8">1Pe 1:8</reference>).<div eID="gen12895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shadow--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.121.5">Psa 121:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.4.6">Is 4:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.4">25:4</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">32:2</reference>). Jesus Christ interposes the shadow of His cross between the blazing rays of justice and us sinners.<div eID="gen12896" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12897" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fruit--</hi>Faith plucks it (<reference osisRef="Prov.3.18">Pr 3:18</reference>). Man lost the tree of life (<reference osisRef="Gen.3.22">Ge 3:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Gen.3.23">23</reference>). Jesus Christ regained it for him; he eats it partly now (<reference osisRef="Ps.119.103">Psa 119:103</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.6.55">Joh 6:55</reference>, <reference osisRef="John.6.57">57</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.2.3">1Pe 2:3</reference>); fully hereafter (<reference osisRef="Rev.2.7">Re 2:7</reference>; 22:2, 14); not earned by the sweat of his brow, or by his righteousness (<reference osisRef="Rom.10.1-Rom.10.21">Ro 10:1-21</reference>). Contrast the worldling's fruit (<reference osisRef="Deut.32.32">De 32:32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.15.16">Lu 15:16</reference>). <div eID="gen12897" type="x-p"/>
entries.3b514d739910ecf579069f3fe53cd7fca1020f7a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8212"/><div sID="gen12898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8212"/>4. Historically fulfilled in the joy of Simeon and Anna in the temple, over the infant Saviour (<reference osisRef="Luke.2.25-Luke.2.38">Lu 2:25-38</reference>), and that of Mary, too (compare <reference osisRef="Luke.1.53">Lu 1:53</reference>); typified (<reference osisRef="Exod.24.9-Exod.24.11">Ex 24:9-11</reference>). Spiritually, the bride or beloved is led (<reference osisRef="Song.2.4">So 2:4</reference>) first into the King's chambers, thence is drawn after Him in answer to her prayer; is next received on a grassy couch under a cedar kiosk; and at last in a "banqueting hall," such as, Josephus says, Solomon had in his palace, "wherein all the vessels were of gold" (Antiquities, 8:5,2). The transition is from holy retirement to public ordinances, church worship, and the Lord's Supper (<reference osisRef="Ps.36.8">Psa 36:8</reference>). The bride, as the queen of Sheba, is given "all her desire" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.10.13">1Ki 10:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.63.5">Psa 63:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.3.8">Ep 3:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eph.3.16-Eph.3.21">16-21</reference>; <reference osisRef="Phil.4.19">Php 4:19</reference>); type of the heavenly feast hereafter (<reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Is 25:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.25.9">9</reference>).<div eID="gen12898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his banner ... love--</hi>After having rescued us from the enemy, our victorious captain (<reference osisRef="Heb.2.10">He 2:10</reference>) seats us at the banquet under a banner inscribed with His name, "love" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.8">1Jo 4:8</reference>). His love conquered us to Himself; this banner rallies round us the forces of Omnipotence, as our protection; it marks to what country we belong, heaven, the abode of love, and in what we most glory, the cross of Jesus Christ, through which we triumph (<reference osisRef="Rom.8.37">Ro 8:37</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.15.57">1Co 15:57</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Re 3:21</reference>). Compare with "over me," "underneath are the everlasting arms" (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.27">De 33:27</reference>). <div eID="gen12899" type="x-p"/>
entries.026745c187843b6dd4bd55025e375ba5742cfd68: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8213"/><div sID="gen12900" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8213"/><hi type="bold">5. flagons--</hi>Maurer prefers translating, "dried raisin cakes"; from the Hebrew root "fire," namely, dried by heat. But the "house of wine" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.4">So 2:4</reference>, Margin) favors "flagons"; the "new wine" of the kingdom, the Spirit of Jesus Christ.<div eID="gen12900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">apples--</hi>from the tree (<reference osisRef="Song.2.3">So 2:3</reference>), so sweet to her, the promises of God.<div eID="gen12901" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12902" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">sick of love--</hi>the highest degree of sensible enjoyment that can be attained here. It may be at an early or late stage of experience. Paul (<reference osisRef="2Cor.12.7">2Co 12:7</reference>). In the last sickness of J. Welch, he was overheard saying, "Lord, hold thine hand, it is enough; thy servant is a clay vessel, and can hold no more" [Fleming, Fulfilling of the Scriptures]. In most cases this intensity of joy is reserved for the heavenly banquet. Historically, Israel had it, when the Lord's glory filled the tabernacle, and afterwards the temple, so that the priests could not stand to minister: so in the Christian Church on Pentecost. The bride addresses Christ mainly, though in her rapture she uses the plural, "Stay (ye) me," speaking generally. So far from asking the withdrawal of the manifestations which had overpowered her, she asks for more: so "fainteth for" (<reference osisRef="Ps.84.2">Psa 84:2</reference>): also Peter, on the mount of transfiguration (<reference osisRef="Luke.9.33">Lu 9:33</reference>), "Let us make ... not knowing what he said." <div eID="gen12902" type="x-p"/>
entries.a77abe8baf71e3d4abb53da1faab270509b90f31: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8214"/><div sID="gen12903" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8214"/>6. The "stay" she prayed for (<reference osisRef="Song.2.5">So 2:5</reference>) is granted (<reference osisRef="Deut.33.12">De 33:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Deut.33.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.37.24">Psa 37:24</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.41.16">Is 41:16</reference>). None can pluck from that embrace (<reference osisRef="John.10.28-John.10.30">Joh 10:28-30</reference>). His hand keeps us from falling (<reference osisRef="Matt.14.30">Mt 14:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.14.31">31</reference>); to it we may commit ourselves (<reference osisRef="Ps.31.5">Psa 31:5</reference>).<div eID="gen12903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">left hand--</hi>the left is the inferior hand, by which the Lord less signally manifests His love, than by the right; the secret hand of ordinary providence, as distinguished from that of manifested grace (the "right"). They really go together, though sometimes they seem divided; here both are felt at once. Theodoret takes the left hand, equivalent to judgment and wrath; the right, equivalent to honor and love. The hand of justice no longer is lifted to smite, but is under the head of the believer to support (<reference osisRef="Isa.42.21">Is 42:21</reference>); the hand of Jesus Christ pierced by justice for our sin supports us. The charge not to disturb the beloved occurs thrice: but the sentiment here, "His left hand," &c., nowhere else fully; which accords with the intensity of joy (<reference osisRef="Song.2.5">So 2:5</reference>) found nowhere else; in <reference osisRef="Song.8.3">So 8:3</reference>, it is only conditional, "should embrace," not "doth." <div eID="gen12904" type="x-p"/>
entries.e47e5da0fb85f24455bfe923faa7cae85cd8916a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8215"/><div sID="gen12905" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8215"/><hi type="bold">7. by the roes--</hi>not an oath but a solemn charge, to act as cautiously as the hunter would with the wild roes, which are proverbially timorous; he must advance with breathless circumspection, if he is to take them; so he who would not lose Jesus Christ and His Spirit, which is easily grieved and withdrawn, must be tender of conscience and watchful (<reference osisRef="Ezek.16.43">Eze 16:43</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.4.30">Ep 4:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eph.5.15">5:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.19">1Th 5:19</reference>). In Margin, title of <reference osisRef="Ps.22.1">Psa 22:1</reference>, Jesus Christ is called the "Hind of the morning," hunted to death by the dogs (compare <reference osisRef="Song.2.8">So 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.9">9</reference>, where He is represented as bounding on the hills, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.33">Psa 18:33</reference>). Here He is resting, but with a repose easily broken (<reference osisRef="Zeph.3.17">Zep 3:17</reference>). It is thought a gross rudeness in the East to awaken one sleeping, especially a person of rank.<div eID="gen12905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">my love--</hi>in Hebrew, feminine for masculine, the abstract for concrete, Jesus Christ being the embodiment of love itself (<reference osisRef="Song.3.5">So 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Song.8.7">8:7</reference>), where, as here, the context requires it to be applied to Him, not her. She too is "love" (<reference osisRef="Song.7.6">So 7:6</reference>), for His love calls forth her love. Presumption in the convert is as grieving to the Spirit as despair. The lovingness and pleasantness of the hind and roe (<reference osisRef="Prov.5.19">Pr 5:19</reference>) is included in this image of Jesus Christ.<div eID="gen12906" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12907" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Canticle II.--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Song.2.8-Song.3.5">So 2:8-3:5</reference>)--John the Baptist's Ministry. <div eID="gen12907" type="x-p"/>
entries.143e35a526022144798d005f1d1f94eded6fb327: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8216"/><div sID="gen12908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8216"/><hi type="bold">8. voice--</hi>an exclamation of joyful surprise, evidently after a long silence. The restlessness of sin and fickleness in her had disturbed His rest with her, which she had professed not to wish disturbed "till He should please." He left her, but in sovereign grace unexpectedly heralds His return. She awakes, and at once recognizes His voice (<reference osisRef="1Sam.3.9">1Sa 3:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Sam.3.10">10</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.10.4">Joh 10:4</reference>); her sleep is not so sinfully deep as in <reference osisRef="Song.5.2">So 5:2</reference>.<div eID="gen12908" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12909" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">leaping--</hi>bounding, as the roe does, over the roughest obstacles (<reference osisRef="2Sam.2.18">2Sa 2:18</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.12.8">1Ch 12:8</reference>); as the father of the prodigal "had compassion and ran" (<reference osisRef="Luke.15.20">Lu 15:20</reference>).<div eID="gen12909" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12910" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">upon the hills--</hi>as the sunbeams glancing from hill to hill. So Margin, title of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Ps.22.1">Psa 22:1</reference>), "Hind of the morning" (type of His resurrection). Historically, the coming of the kingdom of heaven (the gospel dispensation), announced by John Baptist, is meant; it primarily is the garden or vineyard; the bride is called so in a secondary sense. "The voice" of Jesus Christ is indirect, through "the friend of the bridegroom" (<reference osisRef="John.3.29">Joh 3:29</reference>), John the Baptist. Personally, He is silent during John's ministration, who awoke the long slumbering Church with the cry. "Every hill shall be made low," in the spirit of Elias, on the "rent mountains" (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.11">1Ki 19:11</reference>; compare <reference osisRef="Isa.52.7">Is 52:7</reference>). Jesus Christ is implied as coming with intense desire (<reference osisRef="Luke.22.15">Lu 22:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.7">He 10:7</reference>), disregarding the mountain hindrances raised by man's sin. <div eID="gen12910" type="x-p"/>
entries.5d4db91b6ae43c1af17713a7d87fca9b9223aa77: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8217"/><div sID="gen12911" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8217"/><hi type="bold">9. he standeth--</hi>after having bounded over the intervening space like a roe. He often stands near when our unbelief hides Him from us (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.16">Ge 28:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.14-Rev.3.20">Re 3:14-20</reference>). His usual way; long promised and expected; sudden at last: so, in visiting the second temple (Mal 3:1); so at Pentecost (<reference osisRef="Acts.2.1">Ac 2:1</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.2">2</reference>); so in visiting an individual soul, Zaccheus (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.5">Lu 19:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.6">6</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.3.8">Joh 3:8</reference>); and so, at the second coming (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.48">Mt 24:48</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.24.50">50</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.4">2Pe 3:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Pet.3.10">10</reference>). So it shall be at His second coming (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.2">1Th 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Thess.5.3">3</reference>).<div eID="gen12911" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12912" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">wall--</hi>over the cope of which He is first seen; next, He looks through (not forth; for He is outside) at the windows, glancing suddenly and stealthily (not as English Version, "showing Himself") through the lattice. The prophecies, types, &c., were lattice glimpses of Him to the Old Testament Church, in spite of the wall of separation which sin had raised (<reference osisRef="John.8.56">Joh 8:56</reference>); clearer glimpses were given by John Baptist, but not unclouded (<reference osisRef="John.1.26">Joh 1:26</reference>). The legal wall of partition was not to be removed until His death (<reference osisRef="Eph.2.14">Ep 2:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.15">15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.20">He 10:20</reference>). Even now, He is only seen by faith, through the windows of His Word and the lattice of ordinances and sacraments (<reference osisRef="Luke.24.35">Lu 24:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="John.14.21">Joh 14:21</reference>); not full vision (<reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>); an incentive to our looking for His second coming (<reference osisRef="Isa.33.17">Is 33:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Titus.2.13">Tit 2:13</reference>). <div eID="gen12912" type="x-p"/>
entries.104a50bb1050439310750311b4ebe03f265f0779: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8218"/><div sID="gen12913" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8218"/>10-11. Loving reassurance given by Jesus Christ to the bride, lest she should think that He had ceased to love her, on account of her unfaithfulness, which had occasioned His temporary withdrawal. He allures her to brighter than worldly joys (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">Mi 2:10</reference>). Not only does the saint wish to depart to be with Him, but He still more desires to have the saint with Him above (<reference osisRef="John.17.24">Joh 17:24</reference>). Historically, the vineyard or garden of the King, here first introduced, is "the kingdom of heaven preached" by John the Baptist, before whom "the law and the prophets were" (<reference osisRef="Luke.16.16">Lu 16:16</reference>). <div eID="gen12913" type="x-p"/>
entries.5fe96342ca2afbd2eea84b6cd36c624fc836bcf0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8220"/><div sID="gen12916" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8220"/><hi type="bold">12. flowers--</hi>tokens of anger past, and of grace come. "The summoned bride is welcome," say some fathers, "to weave from them garlands of beauty, wherewith she may adorn herself to meet the King." Historically, the flowers, &c., only give promise; the fruit is not ripe yet; suitable to the preaching of John the Baptist, "The kingdom of heaven is at hand"; not yet fully come.<div eID="gen12916" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12917" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the time of ... singing--</hi>the rejoicing at the advent of Jesus Christ. Gregory Nyssenus refers the voice of the turtledove to John the Baptist. It with the olive branch announced to Noah that "the rain was over and gone" (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.11">Ge 8:11</reference>). So John the Baptist, spiritually. Its plaintive "voice" answers to his preaching of repentance (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.6">Jr 8:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">7</reference>). Vulgate and Septuagint translate, "The time of pruning," namely, spring (<reference osisRef="John.15.2">Joh 15:2</reference>). The mention of the "turtle's" cooing better accords with our text. The turtledove is migratory (<reference osisRef="Jer.8.7">Jr 8:7</reference>), and "comes" early in May; emblem of love, and so of the Holy Ghost. Love, too, shall be the keynote of the "new song" hereafter (<reference osisRef="Isa.35.10">Is 35:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Re 1:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.14.3">14:3</reference>; 19:6). In the individual believer now, joy and love are here set forth in their earlier manifestations (<reference osisRef="Mark.4.28">Mr 4:28</reference>). <div eID="gen12917" type="x-p"/>
entries.7756de1669bf0c639d43a2a3be638fd7bbe991b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8221"/><div sID="gen12918" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8221"/><hi type="bold">13. putteth forth--</hi>rather, "ripens," literally, "makes red" [Maurer]. The unripe figs, which grow in winter, begin to ripen in early spring, and in June are fully matured [Weiss].<div eID="gen12918" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12919" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">vines with the tender grape--</hi>rather, "the vines in flower," literally, "a flower," in apposition with "vines" [Maurer]. The vine flowers were so sweet that they were often put, when dried, into new wine to give it flavor. Applicable to the first manifestations of Jesus Christ, "the true Vine," both to the Church and to individuals; as to Nathanael under the fig tree (<reference osisRef="John.1.48">Joh 1:48</reference>).<div eID="gen12919" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12920" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Arise, &c.--</hi>His call, described by the bride, ends as it began (<reference osisRef="Song.2.10">So 2:10</reference>); it is a consistent whole; "love" from first to last (<reference osisRef="Isa.52.1">Is 52:1</reference>, 2; <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.17">2Co 6:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.6.18">18</reference>). "Come," in the close of <reference osisRef="Rev.22.17">Re 22:17</reference>, as at His earlier manifestation (<reference osisRef="Matt.11.28">Mt 11:28</reference>). <div eID="gen12920" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e01bca554c83b90c719210f5118dc3bd88f9c7d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8222"/><div sID="gen12921" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8222"/><hi type="bold">14. dove--</hi>here expressing endearment (<reference osisRef="Ps.74.19">Psa 74:19</reference>). Doves are noted for constant attachment; emblems, also, in their soft, plaintive note, of softened penitents (<reference osisRef="Isa.59.11">Is 59:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ezek.7.16">Eze 7:16</reference>); other points of likeness are their beauty; "their wings covered with silver and gold" (<reference osisRef="Ps.68.13">Psa 68:13</reference>), typifying the change in the converted; the dove-like spirit, breathed into the saint by the Holy Ghost, whose emblem is the dove; the messages of peace from God to sinful men, as Noah's dove, with the olive branch (<reference osisRef="Gen.8.11">Ge 8:11</reference>), intimated that the flood of wrath was past; timidity, fleeing with fear from sin and self to the cleft Rock of Ages (<reference osisRef="Isa.26.4">Is 26:4</reference>, Margin; <reference osisRef="Hos.11.11">Ho 11:11</reference>); gregarious, flocking together to the kingdom of Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.8">Is 60:8</reference>); harmless simplicity (<reference osisRef="Matt.10.16">Mt 10:16</reference>).<div eID="gen12921" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12922" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">clefts--</hi>the refuge of doves from storm and heat (<reference osisRef="Jer.48.28">Jr 48:28</reference>; see <reference osisRef="Jer.49.16">Jr 49:16</reference>). Gesenius translates the Hebrew from a different root, "the refuges." But see, for "clefts," <reference osisRef="Exod.33.18-Exod.33.23">Ex 33:18-23</reference>. It is only when we are in Christ Jesus that our "voice is sweet (in prayer, <reference osisRef="Song.4.3">So 4:3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Song.4.11">11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.10.20">Mt 10:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gal.4.6">Ga 4:6</reference>, because it is His voice in us; also in speaking of Him, Mal 3:16); and our countenance comely" (<reference osisRef="Exod.34.29">Ex 34:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.27.5">Psa 27:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.71.3">71:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.33.16">Is 33:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.3.18">2Co 3:18</reference>).<div eID="gen12922" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12923" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">stairs--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ezek.38.20">Eze 38:20</reference>, Margin), a steep rock, broken into stairs or terraces. It is in "secret places" and rugged scenes that Jesus Christ woos the soul from the world to Himself (<reference osisRef="Mic.2.10">Mi 2:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Cor.7.14">7:14</reference>). So Jacob amid the stones of Beth-el (<reference osisRef="Gen.28.11-Gen.28.19">Ge 28:11-19</reference>); Moses at Horeb (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.1-Exod.3.22">Ex 3:1-22</reference>); so Elijah (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.19.9-1Kgs.19.13">1Ki 19:9-13</reference>); Jesus Christ with the three disciples on a "high mountain apart," at the transfiguration (<reference osisRef="Matt.17.1">Mt 17:1</reference>); John in Patmos (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.9">Re 1:9</reference>). "Of the eight beatitudes, five have an afflicted condition for their subject. As long as the waters are on the earth, we dwell in the ark; but when the land is dry, the dove itself will be tempted to wander" [Jeremy Taylor]. Jesus Christ does not invite her to leave the rock, but in it (Himself), yet in holy freedom to lay aside the timorous spirit, look up boldly as accepted in Him, pray, praise, and confess Him (in contrast to her shrinking from being looked at, <reference osisRef="Song.1.6">So 1:6</reference>), (<reference osisRef="Eph.6.19">Ep 6:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.13.15">He 13:15</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.4.18">1Jo 4:18</reference>); still, though trembling, the voice and countenance of the soul in Jesus Christ are pleasant to Him. The Church found no cleft in the Sinaitic legal rock, though good in itself, wherein to hide; but in Jesus Christ stricken by God for us, as the rock smitten by Moses (<reference osisRef="Num.20.11">Nu 20:11</reference>), there is a hiding-place (<reference osisRef="Isa.32.2">Is 32:2</reference>). She praised His "voice" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.8">So 2:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Cor.2.10">10</reference>); it is thus that her voice also, though tremulous, is "sweet" to Him here. <div eID="gen12923" type="x-p"/>
entries.6164c0af9b7d256242a425399bde46c4f86a0079: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8223"/><div sID="gen12924" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8223"/>15. Transition to the vineyard, often formed in "stairs" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.14">So 2:14</reference>), or terraces, in which, amidst the vine leaves, foxes hid.<div eID="gen12924" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12925" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">foxes--</hi>generic term, including jackals. They eat only grapes, not the vine flowers; but they need to be driven out in time before the grape is ripe. She had failed in watchfulness before (<reference osisRef="Song.1.6">So 1:6</reference>); now when converted, she is the more jealous of subtle sins (<reference osisRef="Ps.139.23">Psa 139:23</reference>). In spiritual winter certain evils are frozen up, as well as good; in the spring of revivals these start up unperceived, crafty, false teachers, spiritual pride, uncharitableness, &c. (<reference osisRef="Ps.19.12">Psa 19:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.26">Mt 13:26</reference>; <reference osisRef="Luke.8.14">Lu 8:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.17">2Ti 2:17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.15">He 12:15</reference>). "Little" sins are parents of the greatest (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.1">Ec 10:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.5.6">1Co 5:6</reference>). Historically, John the Baptist spared not the fox-like Herod (<reference osisRef="Luke.13.32">Lu 13:32</reference>), who gave vine-like promise of fruit at first (<reference osisRef="Mark.6.20">Mr 6:20</reference>), at the cost of his life; nor the viper-Sadducees, &c.; nor the varied subtle forms of sin (<reference osisRef="Luke.3.7-Luke.3.14">Lu 3:7-14</reference>). <div eID="gen12925" type="x-p"/>
entries.45877239cca546c90f3ad74392b566adad1bb2fc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8224"/><div sID="gen12926" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8224"/><hi type="bold">16. mine ... his--</hi>rather, "is for me ... for Him" (<reference osisRef="Hos.3.3">Ho 3:3</reference>), where, as here, there is the assurance of indissoluble union, in spite of temporary absence. <reference osisRef="Song.2.17">So 2:17</reference>, entreating Him to return, shows that He has gone, perhaps through her want of guarding against the "little sins" (<reference osisRef="Song.2.15">So 2:15</reference>).
